newsitem.title: USA: Democrats narrow the gap in Louisiana House race.
newsitem.headline: Democrats narrow the gap in Louisiana House race.

text.p: A Republican candidate for a House seat said Saturday he would end his challenge of a primary result after a district court ruled against him, leaving two Democrats in the Nov. 5 race for the southwest Louisiana district.
Since the seat will now go to a Democrat, the Democratic Party is assured of no net losses in the state in the U.S. House of Representatives.
The Democrats could also pick up one of the 19 seats needed to retake control of the House from the Republican majority in another contested election in the state.
A state district court judge late Friday threw out Republican David Thibodaux's suit challenging the electoral results for the 7th district seat, which left him in third place by just 12 votes.

Under Louisiana's unique open primary system, the top two primary vote-getters compete in the runoff, regardless of party affiliation. The 7th District was held by Republican Representative Jimmy Hayes, who ran unsuccessfully for the Senate.

A Democrat and a Republican are also vying for the 4th Congressional District seat in northwest Louisiana that had been held by Democratic Representative Cleo Fields. That district was redrawn by the courts after rulings that it was racially gerrymandered to create a minority-majority district. Fields did not seek re-election.
If a Democrat wins in the 4th district, the state will be split 4-3 in favour of Republicans compared with 5-2 currently, giving the Democrats the additional House seat.

Thibodaux initially was named as the runoff candidate against Democrat Chris John in the primary, but when voting machines were opened three days later, Democrat Hunter Lundy picked up an eight-vote lead. On the recount, it widened to 12.
Thibodaux said Saturday he does not plan to appeal the court ruling throwing out his suit.

"Louisiana's open primary system is an electoral process that already has been declared unconstitutional," Thibodaux said. "While the rest of the country is participating on Nov. 5th in a national referendum on the Republican revolution, voters in the 7th District are just holding a Democratic primary."
Lundy, a political newcomer who calls himself a conservative Democrat, said the week of controversy stemming from the contested primary results have ended his problems with name recognition.
Even without a Republican in the runoff, "the Republican voters realise they have a clear opportunity to make a difference in this election," he said. "I hope they'll come to me."
